claims.text: Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu HEA nanoparticles exhibit local atomic segregation at their surfaces.
Surface segregation creates regions with reduced effective melting points.
The reduced-melting-point surface regions cause premelting to begin at lower temperatures than in monometallic or bimetallic nanoparticles.
The initial Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles are solid, single-phase, homogeneous solid solutions.
Rapid cooling from a melt can preserve a homogeneous multielement solid-solution nanoparticle without segregation or phase separation.
Surface effects are pronounced in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles from a few nanometers to approximately 20 nm.
Local compositional fluctuations and surface segregation produce heterogeneous regions with lower local surface energies.
The chemical complexity of HEA nanoparticles leads to a nonuniform distribution of constituent atoms.
Some surface sites become enriched in one or a few low-surface-energy elements.
Enrichment in low-surface-energy elements reduces the local melting point.
Upon heating, compositionally enriched surface regions premelt before the rest of the particle.
Localized premelting will be observable as surface roughening and early diffraction-peak changes.

Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu HEA nanoparticles will show a statistically significant earlier onset of surface disorder and localized melting than Cu or Cu–Ni nanoparticles prepared and tested under the same conditions.
Earlier localized melting will produce diffraction-peak shifts or broadening and visible TEM surface roughening.
The proposed mechanism is most relevant to sufficiently small nanoparticles with high surface-to-volume ratios.
Rapid heating near the premelting regime enhances the relevance of the proposed segregation-controlled mechanism.
The proposed effect becomes less pronounced for larger particles or during slow heating because bulk behavior dominates.
